title: 0. Executive Thesis, Dual Verdict & Opportunity Matrix

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: grade the business first and the price second, because a great company bought at the wrong moment still hurts.
epigraph.author: Portfolio Desk Charter

web_blocks.html: What the company actually does. MPS Limited (NSE: MPSLTD; BSE 532440) turns research manuscripts, school and nursing textbooks and corporate training into finished digital products. Its customers are the world's largest publishers, universities, health systems and corporations [1]. It reports three segments. Research Solutions is 60% of FY26 revenue and about two-thirds of segment profit. It runs peer review, production and research-integrity work for scholarly publishers on platforms such as DigiCore and HighWire. Education Solutions (27%) builds adaptive courseware. Since February 2026 it also owns Unbound Medicine's subscription clinical-reference apps. Corporate Learning (13%) builds custom e-learning and simulations through Tata Interactive, TOPSIM and Liberate [1, 2]. FY26 consolidated revenue was ₹768.37 Cr, EBITDA ₹235.85 Cr and audited basic EPS ₹102.11. Some 99.5% of revenue is earned in foreign currency [1]. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 17.8% to ₹448.5 Cr and EBITDA grew 39% to ₹154 Cr, a 34.3% margin. Management raised the full-year EBITDA floor from ₹300 Cr to at least ₹310 Cr [2].

web_blocks.caption: Executive Decision Matrix: Dual Verdict, Multi-Horizon Posture & Valuation Levels (as of the 12 November 2026 verified close)
web_blocks.takeaway: The business earns a COMPOUNDER_PASS, but the desk does not buy at ₹2,297.00. The probability-weighted 12-month value is ₹2,440 (+6.2%) on current earnings and ₹2,254 (-1.9%) on year-end earnings, and reward-to-risk to the ₹2,005 invalidation level is 0.39:1 or worse. The tape is at the Stage 3/Stage 4 boundary. On the more generous earnings basis the support zone offers 1.79:1 at ₹2,150 and 5.23:1 at ₹2,070. On year-end earnings it offers 0.63:1 and 2.63:1, so only the ₹2,070 end clears the 1.5:1 hurdle on both. MPSLTD is not held (0 shares), so the only open decision is whether to earmark cash.

web_blocks.html: Why the price is where it is, and our judgment. The stock has run a full cycle inside twelve months. It traded at about 42 times trailing profit in March 2025, 16 times in March 2026, 29 times in August 2026 and 22.7 times now. Over that span earnings per share grew 16% in FY26 and the Q2 FY27 print beat [2]. Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems and Newgen are all in Stage 4 and have fallen 18% to 56% in a year as the market priced AI disruption into content and services names. MPS has held up better than that group but has started to roll over. We think the business deserves a premium to those peers. It earns a 38.7% ROCE against 20% to 25% for them, converts profit to cash, and has repaid its acquisition loan [1]. We also think a payoff below 1:1 is too thin for a stock that has fallen 50% or more three times since 2015. Across three horizons: the short term (1 to 3 months) is WAIT, because the tape offers no edge. The medium term (6 to 18 months) is ACCUMULATE only inside ₹2,070 to ₹2,150 with the ₹2,005 stop, or a re-underwrite after a confirmed Stage 2 re-base. That also needs H2 FY27 EBITDA to keep the ₹310 Cr floor on track and Research margin at or above 45%. The long term (3 to 5 years) is a genuine compounder candidate. The open debate there is price, AI price give-back and acquisition discipline, not whether the franchise exists.

book_paragraphs: This monograph asks two questions in order. First: is MPS a good business? Second: is it a good purchase today? Most investors collapse the two into one and then wonder why a company they admired lost half its value while they held it. We keep them apart on purpose.

Start with the business. MPS began in 1970 as the Indian production unit of a British publisher and became the outsourcing partner that the world's largest scholarly publishers hand their manuscripts to. Picture a researcher in Munich submitting a paper: it goes through peer review, copy-editing, typesetting, tagging for search engines and publication on a journal platform, and a large share of that journey now runs on MPS's people and software. The company earns about ₹30 of EBITDA on every ₹100 of sales, converts that into cash almost one-for-one over ten years, and has no bank debt after repaying its Unbound Medicine loan this August.

Now the price. At ₹2,297 on 12 November, the shares trade at about 22.7 times last year's profit. That is neither cheap nor expensive against the last five years. It is cheap compared with the 42 times the market paid in March 2025, and dear compared with the 16 times it paid twelve months later. The reverse DCF says the market already assumes the company's free cash flow grows around 9% a year for a decade, which is below what MPS has delivered since FY21, so the price is not demanding. Why not buy, then?

Because the payoff has to be asymmetric before we put money to work, and at this price it is not. Our probability-weighted value is ₹2,440, a 6.2% gain, and our base value of ₹2,410 is only 5% above the price. The gain to that base value is a third of the loss to our invalidation level at ₹2,005. If the shares fall to the ₹2,070 to ₹2,150 zone, where the rising 200-day average and the last swing low sit, the arithmetic improves. At ₹2,070 it gives about five rupees of reward for each rupee at risk on current earnings and 2.6 on year-end earnings. At ₹2,150 it gives 1.8 and 0.6, so we treat ₹2,150 as conditional. That is the entire verdict: a good business, a fair price and a payoff that improves if we are patient, with the first purchase kept small.

Two sentences from management's November call frame what we are waiting to see. The chief financial officer, Prarthana Agarwal, said: "We are now raising the floor, and we expect FY27 EBITDA to be at least INR310 crores." The chief executive, Rahul Arora, added about acquisitions: "I would rather miss a deal than overpay." We are applying the same discipline to the shares that he says he applies to deals.

book_callouts.title: PROLOGUE BRIEFING: WHAT WOULD CHANGE OUR MIND
book_callouts.quote: A compounder is a good purchase only when the price leaves room for the business to be a little wrong.
book_callouts.text: MPS is a WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT today. Three things would move the file, and one thing would cancel it.
bullets: Price: a fall to ₹2,070 with the ₹2,005 invalidation intact earns a first fill of about 2.17% of net worth. A further 1.08% at ₹2,150 follows only if the re-derived base value is at least ₹2,367.50 on year-end earnings.
Tape: a weekly close above the falling 50-day average near ₹2,500 on rising volume, with the 30-week average rising, re-opens the file for a fresh valuation and stop review. It is not a buy signal.
Evidence: H2 FY27 EBITDA tracking at least ₹156 Cr, Research margin at or above 45% and Corporate Learning above 18% keep the business case intact.
Cancel: a daily close below ₹2,005, Research margin under 42% for two quarters, the largest customer above 20%, or a goodwill impairment above ₹25 Cr.

book_subsections.title: Why a 22.7x multiple is not a bargain and not a bubble
paragraphs: Multiples confuse people because they look like facts. They are really opinions about how long a stream of cash will last. In MPS's case the opinion has swung widely. Using the profit of the last reported fiscal year, the shares traded at under 5 times earnings at the March 2020 low, at 41.7 times in March 2025, at 16.0 times in March 2026 and at 28.9 times in August 2026. Over the last decade the median is 17.6 times, and over the last five years it is 22.7 times. Today's 22.7 times therefore equals the recent median and sits a little above the decade's.

What does that tell you? That the market is not paying a fear discount, and it is not paying a euphoria premium. It is paying about what it has typically paid in the AI era for a business with 38.7% returns on capital. The enterprise value is about ₹3,784 crore after netting out ₹163 crore of cash, which is roughly 12 times the EBITDA we expect for FY27. The Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems and Newgen peers trade on lower or similar multiples with much lower returns on capital, and all three are in downtrends.

So the valuation does not argue for stepping back. The tape does. The shares are below a falling 50-day average, they sit on the 30-week average that separates Stage 3 from Stage 4, nine of the last 25 sessions were distribution days, and daily volume has dried up to a third of its normal level. Four things confirm each other, and none of them says that buyers are in charge. The disciplined response is to name the price at which the maths pays us properly, set the stop where the idea is wrong, and let the stock come to us.
